Benefits and uses

PT-141 benefits and uses

PT-141 (bremelanotide) has one FDA-approved use: as Vyleesi, for premenopausal women with acquired, generalized HSDD.2 In two 24-week phase 3 trials of 1,267 such women, it raised desire scores and lowered distress about low desire more than placebo, by small margins.1 It did not increase satisfying sexual events.2 Evidence in men comes from small studies.34

What the phase 3 trials found

The main evidence comes from two identical 24-week phase 3 trials, RECONNECT studies 301 and 302.1 They randomized 1,267 premenopausal women with acquired, generalized HSDD to bremelanotide or placebo.1 Participants had a mean age of 39, and 86% were white and 12% Black.2

Outcome over 24 weeks Result versus placebo
Sexual desire score (FSFI desire domain) 0.30 points higher in study 301, 0.42 in study 302, 0.35 pooled1
Distress about low desire 0.37 points lower in study 301, 0.29 in study 3021
Women rating themselves as benefiting (5 or more on a 1 to 7 scale) 58.3% and 58.2%, versus 36.1% and 35.4% on placebo1
Satisfying sexual events No significant difference2

In the label's own analysis, desire scores rose 0.5 and 0.6 points with Vyleesi versus 0.2 with placebo.2

What the outcome measures mean

  • Desire score: the FSFI desire domain runs from 1.2 to 6, and higher means more desire.2 A gain of about 0.3 to 0.4 points over placebo is a small shift on that range.12
  • Distress score: a single question on distress about low desire over the past 30 days, answered from 0 (never) to 4 (always).2 It fell 0.7 points with Vyleesi versus 0.4 with placebo in both studies.2
  • Responder threshold: the label counted a desire gain of at least 1.2 points as a response.2 The share of women who reached it appears only in label figures.
  • Satisfying sexual events: a secondary endpoint. Mean changes were 0.0 versus a drop of 0.1 in study 1 (p = 0.76), and 0.0 versus 0.0 in study 2 (p = 0.70).2
  • Global benefit: one question scored from 1 (very much worse) to 7 (very much better), where 5 or more counted as benefit.1

Limits of the trials

More women on bremelanotide than on placebo left the blinded phase early: 40% versus 13% in study 1, and 39% versus 25% in study 2.2 The trial authors list this uneven withdrawal, and a mostly white study group, as limitations.1 The results apply to premenopausal women only. Effectiveness after menopause has not been established.1

How independent reviewers read the results

A 2021 re-analysis found that 72.72% of the outcomes listed in the trial protocols were not reported in the main paper.9 A 2024 follow-up judged the effects nil to small.10 It called the benefits statistically modest and limited to outcomes with scant evidence of validity in women with HSDD.10 The trial investigators published a commentary disputing the 2021 re-analysis.11 Readers weighing the evidence should know both views exist.

Weighing benefit against side effects

In the same trials, about 58% of women on bremelanotide rated themselves as benefiting, against about 36% on placebo.1 Over the same 24 weeks, 40% had nausea, 20.3% had flushing and 11.3% had headache.2 Side effects led 18% to stop, versus 2% on placebo.2 Claims that PT-141 works with few side effects do not match these label figures. The label's stopping rule applies when a patient reports no improvement after 8 weeks.2

Earlier and longer studies in women

  • Dose-finding trial (12 weeks, 2016): in premenopausal women with sexual dysfunction, the combined 1.25 and 1.75 mg groups gained 0.7 satisfying sexual events a month, versus 0.2 on placebo (p = 0.018).8
  • Open-label extension (52 weeks): of 684 women who entered, 272 completed it. The authors reported sustained improvement and no new safety signals.7

Findings in men

Small placebo-controlled studies from 2004 found erectile responses after injected or nasal doses in healthy men and in men with erectile dysfunction.34 In a 2005 crossover study of 19 men with erectile dysfunction, low-dose nasal PT-141 given with sildenafil produced a greater erectile response than sildenafil alone.12 A 2008 trial in 342 men who had not responded to sildenafil reported positive results in 33.5% on nasal bremelanotide versus 8.5% on placebo.13 The journal attached an expression of concern to it in 2023.13 No use in men is FDA approved.2 Details are on PT-141 and men's health.

Animal and mechanism findings

In female rats, PT-141 selectively increased solicitation (courtship) behavior without changing lordosis, pacing or other sexual behaviors.14 Given to rats and nonhuman primates, it caused penile erections, according to a 2003 paper.15 A 2022 review proposes that it acts on MC4 receptors in the hypothalamus to raise dopamine release, a model built mainly on animal work.16 The label itself states that the mechanism in women with HSDD is unknown.2 Animal results do not show that the same effects occur in people.

What has not been shown

  • Benefit after menopause: not established, and the label does not cover postmenopausal women.12
  • Energy, mood or tanning: the trials did not measure these as benefits, and skin darkening is a labeled side effect, not a goal.2
  • Benefit in men: no study in men has led to an approval, and the largest trial in our sources carries an expression of concern.213
  • Comparisons: our sources include no head-to-head trial against sildenafil or flibanserin.

Frequently asked questions

Does PT-141 increase energy?

The phase 3 trials measured sexual desire, distress about low desire and satisfying sexual events, not energy.25 Fatigue was in fact reported slightly more often with Vyleesi (3.2%) than with placebo (0.5%).2 No source reviewed for this page reports an energy benefit, so claims that PT-141 boosts energy are not supported by the published trials.

Does PT-141 improve mood?

Mood was not an efficacy outcome in the phase 3 trials, which measured desire and distress about low desire.2 The trial report says depression and suicidal thinking were tracked for safety, with no clinically significant effects seen.1 MedlinePlus says bremelanotide works by activating natural substances in the brain that control mood and thinking.6 That describes how it may act, not a measured mood benefit. The label adds that the exact way it improves low desire in women is unknown.2

Do the effects of PT-141 last with continued use?

In a 52-week open-label extension of the phase 3 trials, 684 women continued on bremelanotide, and the authors reported sustained improvement in desire and distress.7 Only 272 of them completed the extension, and it was open-label and uncontrolled, so the result is weaker evidence than the blinded trials.72 The label says to stop after 8 weeks if there is no improvement.2

Does PT-141 lead to more sex?

Not in the phase 3 trials. The number of satisfying sexual events, a secondary endpoint, did not differ significantly from placebo.2 An earlier 12-week dose-finding trial in 327 premenopausal women did report a gain of 0.7 satisfying events a month in the combined 1.25 and 1.75 mg groups, versus 0.2 with placebo.8 The two larger phase 3 trials did not show that gain.2
